text:
The Perfect Boy

In college, we called him Q because his name was Quentin and because the letter suited him—round, self-contained, with that little tail flicking off somewhere private. Q was the kind of person about whom others said, without irony, "He's just good at everything," and then felt vaguely accused by the fact of him. He rowed. He played cello late at night, when he thought nobody important was listening. He wrote his economics papers in a single draft, in longhand. He was handsome in a way that did not seem to require maintenance, the way old brick buildings are handsome.

I was his roommate sophomore year, and then his friend, which are different things. As his roommate, I had access to the material evidence of Q: the cello, the stack of index cards on which he copied quotations he found useful. ("What stands in the way becomes the way." He'd gotten that from Marcus Aurelius, a person I associated, at nineteen, exclusively with "Gladiator.") As his friend, I had access to something stranger: the conviction, shared by everyone who knew him, that Q was exempt from the ordinary friction of life.

He got the internships. He got the fellowships. When his girlfriend junior year broke up with him—an event the whole dorm had anticipated, since she was clearly unworthy and he was clearly oblivious—he absorbed it in about four days, during which he went rowing twice and made me a frittata. "She was unhappy," he told me, cracking eggs with one hand. "Unhappy people need different things than I can give them." I remember thinking this was an extraordinarily mature way of describing being dumped, and also that it was, possibly, a little inhuman. There was a quality to Q's equanimity that made you want to test it, the way you want to press on a bruise.

I tested it once. Senior year, drunk at a party, I told him that everyone found him exhausting, that his competence made the rest of us feel like we were failing at some exam he hadn't even studied for. He listened with his head tilted, the way a dog listens to a word it almost knows. Then he said, "I know," and refilled my glass. That was the worst part. He knew.

We lost touch the way people do, gradually and then completely. He went to a consultancy, then a foundation, then something involving international development I could never hold in my head. There was a wedding I wasn't invited to, and then a divorce I heard about thirdhand, with a small, shameful pulse of satisfaction I have never quite forgiven myself for. Q, divorcing. The flawless surface, cracked at last. I imagined the settlement conducted with terrible grace, the frittata made for the lawyer.

I moved to a city he didn't live in, married a woman he never met, took a job in publishing that paid less than it sounded like it did. Years passed. His name came up maybe once every eighteen months, less as news than as a unit of measurement—"He's doing the Q thing," someone would say of a colleague promoted twice in a year, and everyone who had known him would nod.

And then, last August, I saw him at a pool.

I should say it was a hotel pool, and I should say why I was there, because the circumstances matter. My marriage had reached the stage where we took separate vacations by mutual, unspoken agreement—she to her sister's lake house, I to a mid-range hotel two hours from home, chosen for its proximity to nothing. It was a truce. I spent my days reading paperbacks and feeling the sun do its slow damage.

He arrived on my third morning. I knew him immediately, though he was heavier and grayer, his hair retreated to a laurel arrangement around the sides of his head. It was the posture. Nobody else sits at the edge of a hotel pool with that spine. He was on the phone, frowning at the water, and something in the frown stopped me from going over.

Here I must confess something. I did not announce myself. I told myself I was waiting for him to finish his call. But the call ended, and I stayed where I was, half-hidden behind a potted palm. I had been given, unasked, the opportunity to observe Q unobserved—to see him as the world saw him rather than as he arranged himself to be seen—and I took it. It was not my finest hour.

What I observed, over that morning, was a man failing at something.

The woman arrived around ten. She was perhaps forty, briskly dressed in linen pants and a blouse she had no intention of getting wet, and she carried a folder, which at a pool is a kind of cry for help. She sat across from Q at one of the café tables by the snack bar, and though the pool was full of shrieking children, I could hear enough, because Q's voice, when he was uncomfortable, got louder, more formal, as if he were addressing a committee.

It became clear, piece by piece, that this was a work matter, and that the work matter was her. She was being let go, or moved, or passed over—I never got the precise shape of it—and Q was the person who had to tell her. Perhaps he had flown in to tell her.

And he was bad at it. He was so bad at it that I had to put the paperback down and stare at it sightlessly, the way you do when you are eavesdropping and need to look occupied.

"It's a structural realignment," he kept saying, and she kept saying, quietly, "Just tell me, Quentin." He would begin a sentence—"The foundation values—" and she would look at him, and the sentence would die. He tried Marcus Aurelius on her. I swear this is true. He said, "What stands in the way becomes the way," and she said, "Are you firing me with a quotation?" and the color rose in his face in a way I had never seen in four years of living with him—not when his girlfriend left, not when I told him he was exhausting, not ever.

The whole thing took an hour. She cried, briefly and with obvious fury at herself for crying. He offered her a napkin from the snack-bar dispenser, one of those flimsy ones that disintegrate on contact, and it disintegrated on contact, and they both looked at the shreds of it in his hand, and for a moment I thought one of them would laugh, which might have saved everything. Neither did. She left with her folder still closed, which I understood to mean she had come already knowing, and had only wanted to see whether he could say it. He couldn't. That was the news she had actually come for, and she got it.

After she left, Q sat at the little table for a long time. He picked up the napkin shreds one by one. Then he took out his phone, and I watched him compose something, delete it, compose it again. Whoever it was for, I like to think he never sent it. He put the phone away and sat some more, and the sun moved, and his shoulders, which had been so straight, settled into the ordinary slump of a man alone at a hotel pool with a job he was bad at.

I should have gone over then. That was the moment, if there was one. I could have said his name, and watched the old posture reassemble itself, and we could have done the whole performance—my God, how long, you look great, we should get a drink—and it might even have been genuine, underneath.

But I didn't. I have thought about why, and the honest answer is unflattering on both ends. Part of it was that I didn't want him to know I'd seen it—the napkin, the quotation, the slump—and I suspected he would know, somehow, the way he had always known things. Part of it, the part I am least proud of, is that what I had witnessed felt like a gift, and I didn't want to hand it back. For twenty years, Q had been the measure against which I found myself wanting, and now I had spent one morning watching him be wanting, and I was not ready to give up the feeling. It was not a good feeling. But it was mine, and I kept it.

I left the next morning. At checkout, on an impulse I didn't examine, I asked whether a Quentin was still registered. The clerk said he had checked out early, and then, because hotel clerks see everything and tell some of it, she added that he had sat in the lobby for nearly an hour before his car came, not reading, not on his phone, just sitting. "We were a little worried about him," she said.

I drove home. My wife was back from the lake, and we cooked dinner together, and something in the way we moved around each other in the kitchen had eased, a little, for no reason either of us could name. I didn't tell her about the pool. I have told no one until now.

Sometimes I think I should reach out to him. It would be easy; people like Q are never hard to find. But I know how the catching up would go. He would tell me about the foundation, the realignment, the hard year, and he would tell it well, with the rough edges sanded into anecdote, because that is what people like Q do with their failures—they process them into material, they copy them onto index cards, they make frittatas out of them. And the man I saw at the pool, the one picking up shreds of napkin, would vanish back into the letter, the round self-contained Q, and I would be the only one who remembered the little tail flicking off somewhere private.

So I keep the morning instead. It is the truest thing I have of him.
